findings.claim: 01.08 Trader vs Private Seller Classification specifies its entire normative content against EU/UK consumer law, which meta/constraints.md's ratified US-first jurisdiction parameterization forbids as an implicit default — leaving the launch market's actual trader rules unspecified for a classification the same file makes a hard precondition of listing.
findings.evidence: 01.08-trader-status-classification.md:10 — "Under EU/UK consumer law the distinction decides whether a buyer gets a 14-day right of withdrawal, a statutory warranty and a redress route, or none of them; and marketplace operators have duties to collect trader details, display them, and tell buyers plainly when consumer protections do **not** apply." 01.08:25 — "Traders supply and publish: legal name, geographic address, contact details, and (where applicable) a company or VAT number." (VAT is an EU/UK instrument with no US analogue.) 01.08 D-04:85 — "Classification is a precondition of listing; fails closed". CONTRADICTED BY meta/constraints.md:267 — "US has no federal 14-day withdrawal right (unlike EU) — returns are policy-driven per seller." meta/constraints.md:353 — "**Exactly one profile is authored at launch: `US`.** Every other territory — including the UK, ... statutory fields resolve to an explicit `unknown`, never to a silent UK default." The sibling leaf applies exactly this rule: 01.07:100 D-06 — "the UK vocabulary (premises licence, PAT, PLI, TEN) **retires into an unauthored profile rather than remaining the implicit default**". 01.08 is dated 2026-07-17 (line 6); the US-first revision was confirmed 2026-07-18 (constraints.md:248).
findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must invent (a) what triggers trader status in the US launch profile, (b) what a US trader must publish (the file's only concrete list — legal name, geographic address, contact details, VAT number — is the EU/UK set), and (c) what the buyer-facing disclosure says when there is no 14-day withdrawal right to lose. Because D-04 makes classification a fail-closed precondition of every listing in domains 05/13/14, no marketplace listing flow can be built without inventing this.
findings.notCoveredBy: 01.08 Q-02 asks 'Does the classification vary by jurisdiction?' — that frames variance as open while the Behavior section still asserts the EU/UK regime as operative. It does not ask which jurisdiction is the launch baseline; constraints.md already answered that, and this file contradicts the answer.

findings.claim: The domain CX file requires an owner-less org to keep accepting bookings and states it is explicitly not frozen, while 01.03.01 states the same org is frozen and 01.03.03's fail-closed mandate rule makes acceptance impossible — three unmarked statements that cannot all hold.
findings.evidence: identity-profiles-organizations-cx.md:305 (CX-16) — "Critically the org is **not** frozen — other people's bookings depend on it." identity-profiles-organizations-cx.md:314 (CX-16 §5) — "An incoming booking arriving while the org is `ownerless` — **the org must still accept it**; who settles it waits on succession." CONTRADICTED BY 01.03-membership-representation-mandate/01.03.01-membership-records-lifecycle.md:114 (States) — "**Unadministrable** | Zero confirmed full-mandate holders (death, suspension, deletion) | A banner to every member: no one can act for this org ... Read paths continue working — **the org is frozen, not broken**." AND BY 01.03.03-mandate-scope-delegated-authority.md D-05:112 — "Resolution fails closed | An unresolvable mandate must never yield elevated authority", where `book` is one of the seven mandated activities (01.03.03 D-01:108). 01.02.02-organization-creation-lifecycle.md:163 takes the CX side — "It is **not** frozen — other people's bookings depend on it" — so the split runs across three files with no precedence rule on any of them.
findings.forcedInvention: For a single-member or non-band org whose sole owning-mandate holder dies (the case 01.03.01 D-14:173 says this state now governs), the implementer must invent whether an incoming booking is (a) auto-accepted with no authorised actor, (b) queued unaccepted, or (c) rejected. Option (a) requires a booking path that bypasses mandate resolution — inventing a hole in the authority model; (b) and (c) contradict CX-16's 'must still accept it'.
findings.notCoveredBy: 01.03.01 Q-04 covers who succeeds a dead sole mandate holder, not what the org may do while it has none. 01.10 Q-01 covers catalogue administration, not booking acceptance.

Aliases are single-owner by construction.** Alias creation asks 'is anyone else in this?' and routes accordingly | Resolves **Q-01**". 01.01.02 Q-01:165: "**RESOLVED — D-04**: it is a band org. Aliases are single-owner. (Number retained: sub-domain CX-02 and the sub-domain index Q-02 both reference 'Q-01 on 01.01.02'.)" — i.e. the dangling references were known and left unfixed. Unresolved — this is the strongest evidence for Q-01 (shared alias may be an org)." 01.01.03-acting-context-switcher.md:34 (Derivation source #2): "Each alias they own (01.01.02) — **including shared aliases**, subject to 01.01.02 Q-01." 01.01.03:123 (Edge Cases): "Two co-owners of a shared alias act as it simultaneously | Same collision, one level down. Recorded as evidence for 01.01.02 Q-01 (shared alias may be an org) ... shared aliases get the same presence indicator | Presence indicator on shared-alias contexts." findings.forcedInvention: Whether alias→owner is 1:1 or 1:N. That single choice determines the alias ownership model, whether the acting-context derivation must union multiple owners per alias, whether alias-scoped notifications fan out to a set, and whether the shared-occupancy presence indicator (01.01.03 D-11) has a second consumer. 01.01.03:123 cannot be reread as the band case: the row immediately above it (:122) is the band case, and this row is explicitly 'one level down'.
findings.notCoveredBy: 01.01 index Q-02 and 01.01.02 Q-01 are both closed against D-04. No live question asks whether aliases may be co-owned.

findings.claim: This unit's CX file states an attribute-union rule that its own child explicitly labels as corrected, and declares as 'unmodelled' a gap its other child explicitly announces resolving — and the child records that the parent was knowingly left unedited.
findings.evidence: STALE RULE — 01.02-organizations-entity-model-cx.md:32 (CX-01 §1): "**Shared state conflict**: The party owns the attribute values; types declare which attributes apply. **Where two types declare the same attribute, it is one value on the party, not two** — the entity has one address regardless of how many things it is." CORRECTED BY 01.02.01-organization-types-attributes.md:41 (Scope property): "Union collisions are **only** possible on `party` scope ... | DT-04; **corrects parent CX-01 Q1**" and :74: "Two types declare the same attribute name with different meanings (studio hourly rate vs venue hire fee; venue capacity vs rehearsal-room occupancy) | **No collision. Both are `type`-scoped, so both values exist**, each qualified by the type that declares it." STALE STATUS — 01.02-cx:66 (CX-03 §1): "A multi-type entity with divergent terminal states per type is **unmodelled** — `[PENDING — Step 5]`, and it is **the sharpest open question in the sub-domain**." RESOLVED BY 01.02.02-organization-creation-lifecycle.md:112: "**A multi-type entity has one lifecycle state, on the party** (D-17, DT-15) — **resolving the sub-domain CX file's sharpest open question**." ADMISSION — 01.02.01:166: "> **Reconciliation note for Step 6**: DT-09/D-11 answers parent index **Q-03** ... DT-04 **corrects parent CX-01 synthesis answer 1** ... DT-06 supplies the answer parent **CX-04** deferred. **Parent index and CX files were not edited from here.**"
findings.forcedInvention: Whether a multi-type org's overlapping attributes collapse to one value or persist per type. Reading the CX file alone, an implementer models one `capacity` and one `rate` per party and silently merges a studio's hourly rate with a venue's hire fee — the exact collision 01.02.01 DT-04 exists to prevent, on what 01.02.01:12 calls "the most-used data in the platform". Also whether a band+label that stops being a band takes a lifecycle transition or a type removal.
findings.downgradeRationale: Warning rather than blocking: both corrections are stated in the children with an explicit pointer back to the parent ('corrects parent CX-01 Q1', 'resolving the sub-domain CX file's sharpest open question'), so an implementer who reads the children resolves it consistently. The defect is that the CX file carries no supersession marker and the reconciliation note records the omission as deliberate.

findings.claim: 01.02.01 specifies a `floored` returns-policy rule as shipped behaviour — a write rejection plus literal user copy asserting a 14-day cancellation right — for a launch market that constraints.md states has no such right, reproducing the silent-default failure the same file's D-14 was written to forbid.
findings.evidence: 01.02.01-organization-types-attributes.md:82 (Edge Cases) — "A trader's shop publishes a returns policy below the statutory minimum ('no returns, ever') | **Rejected at write.** `floored` authority: the statutory floor for the buyer's jurisdiction is rendered as non-editable platform text; the shop's own field may only add terms more generous than the floor (DT-10) | \"**Buyers have a 14-day right to cancel that you can't remove.** Add your own terms below that.\"" CONTRADICTED BY meta/constraints.md:267 — "Consumer protection / returns | Physical + digital goods | **v1.5** | **US has no federal 14-day withdrawal right (unlike EU)** — returns are policy-driven per seller." The file's own D-14:155 states the governing rule it violates here: "Where it declares none — including every unauthored profile — the field resolves to `preference`, is an Operator claim labelled as a claim, and the bound has **no input** rather than being **silently unenforced**."
findings.forcedInvention: Whether the shop returns-policy field is write-gated at launch and against what floor. An implementer following the Edge Case builds a rejection against a non-existent US federal right and ships copy asserting a legal right buyers do not have; one following D-14 ships the field as `preference` with no bound.
findings.downgradeRationale: Warning rather than blocking: 01.02.01 Q-03 explicitly holds `floored` open — "**Still open for `floored` authority (DT-10)**: the statutory returns floor is a property of the *buyer's* jurisdiction ... and no source states which floors apply" — so the gap is tracked. What is not tracked is that the Edge Cases row already asserts a specific floor and rejection behaviour as current.

findings.claim: The same trigger — an org's sole owning-mandate holder dying, being suspended or deleting their account — produces two differently-named states with two different succession mechanisms in two sibling files, each claiming to close the same cross-cut gap.
findings.evidence: 01.02.02-organization-creation-lifecycle.md:84 — "**Ownership axis**: `unclaimed` -> `owned` -> `ownerless` (involuntary loss only — see D-16) -> `owned`"; D-16:257 — "**Involuntary owner loss (death, account termination) yields `ownerless` + a succession route.**"; :163 (Edge Cases) — "Sole owning mandate holder **dies** ... The org enters `ownerless`; **succession routes via 01.10 (estate) and 01.05.03 (transfer)**." VERSUS 01.03.01-membership-records-lifecycle.md D-14:173 — "An org with zero confirmed full-mandate holders enters **`unadministrable`** and triggers a **succession offer to the longest-tenured remaining member, announced to all, contestable for 14 days** | **Closes the domain CX-09 gap.**"; :72 (Edge Cases) — "The org enters `unadministrable` at the instant authority ends ... A **succession offer** goes to the longest-tenured remaining `confirmed` member ... with a **14-day contest window**."; States:114 — "**Unadministrable** | Zero confirmed full-mandate holders (death, suspension, deletion)". The domain CX attributes the state to 01.02 only: identity-profiles-organizations-cx.md:305 — "01.02 supplies the `ownerless` state and a succession route (D-16); 01.10 supplies the estate."
findings.forcedInvention: Whether the party model carries one state or two, which enum name is canonical, and which succession path fires on a death: 01.02.02's route out to 01.10/01.05.03, or 01.03.01's internal offer-to-longest-tenured with a 14-day contest. The two are not sequenced anywhere, and 01.03.01 D-14 narrows its own scope to '(a) single-member orgs, (b) every non-band org type ... (c) the uncapped owning mandate' — exactly the cases 01.02.02:163 routes outward instead.
findings.downgradeRationale: Warning: the two mechanisms are partly layerable (01.03.01 D-14 does route 'No remaining members -> ... exits to 01.10'), so a careful implementer can compose them. What no file states is that they are the same state under two names, or which name the party record uses.

findings.claim: A shadow party's name may be up to 120 characters and D-13 requires that name to become an alias on claim, but an alias display name is capped at 100 characters — leaving a 20-character band in which a legal shadow name cannot become the alias it is specified to become, at the domain's primary conversion event.
findings.evidence: 01.05.01-shadow-party-creation-invitation.md:43 — "| **Name** | Yes | **1–120 characters**, counted and compared after the name is normalized ..."; D-09:210 — "**A shadow party has no free-text surface** — a name (**<=120 chars**, no URLs, no markup), a creator, structured flow context, an optional contact route and an optional identifier."; D-13:214 — "A shadow party's name is **alias-shaped**, not person-shaped. **Claiming binds it as an alias of a person** — often a person who already exists."; :53 — "the name on a shadow party is **alias-shaped**: on claim it becomes an alias of a person (01.01.02)". CONTRADICTED BY 01.01-person-identity-roles/01.01.02-artist-names-aliases-projects.md:36 — "| **Display name** | **1–100 characters**, full Unicode (music is global: `坂本龍一`, `Sigur Rós`, `†††`). **No uniqueness constraint, ever** (D-05)." Neither file references the other's limit, and 01.01.02's alias-creation contract is all-or-nothing (E-14/E-15:78-79).
findings.forcedInvention: What happens when a 101–120 character shadow name is claimed: truncate the name (mutating a third party's attested reference), reject the claim (blocking the conversion the growth loop exists to produce), widen the alias limit, or create the alias out of spec. All four are defensible and produce different products.
findings.notCoveredBy: 01.05.01 Q-01..Q-04 and 01.01.02 Q-04..Q-08. No question addresses the name-length seam at claim.

findings.claim: 01.04.02 carries a live edge case for a band that is 'a shared alias rather than an org', concluding that name ownership then has no governance home — a scenario 01.01.02 D-04 made unreachable by ratifying that a shared name IS a band org.
findings.evidence: 01.04.02-name-trademark-ownership.md:48 (Edge Cases) — "Band is a shared alias rather than an org (01.01.02 Q-01) | Then name ownership **has no governance home, because aliases have no governance** | `[PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]` — real evidence for 01.01.02 Q-01". CONTRADICTED BY 01.01-person-identity-roles/01.01.02-artist-names-aliases-projects.md D-04:152 — "**A shared name is a band org (01.02.01 type `band`), not a co-owned alias. Aliases are single-owner by construction**" and Q-01:165 — "**RESOLVED — D-04**: it is a band org." The consequence is recorded in the opposite direction at identity-profiles-organizations-cx.md:237 (CX-12) — "Because D-04 makes a shared name a band, 01.04's governance capture must be reachable **from** alias creation" — i.e. the shared-alias case has a governance home by construction, which is the reverse of what this row asserts. 01.04.02 is dated 2026-07-16 (line 6), before the ratification.
findings.forcedInvention: Whether a governance-less shared-name path must be built at all. An implementer following this row builds a name-ownership case for an entity with no governance surface; one following D-04 knows every shared name is a band org and inherits 01.04 governance plus the CX-12 capture-at-alias-creation requirement.
findings.downgradeRationale: Warning rather than blocking: the row's premise is void rather than the specification being contradictory about behaviour, and 01.04.02's Q-01 is otherwise resolved thoroughly. The cost is a dead code path plus a false 'no governance home' claim.

findings.claim: 01.06.03 ratifies the per-recipient EPK link as 'a tracking wrapper over public content, not an access gate' while the same file states the EPK may carry rates and contact routes 'not meant for the world' and lists rates as standard Producer EPK content — leaving the confidentiality status of EPK content undetermined.
findings.evidence: 01.06.03-epk-generation-sharing.md D-06:97 — "**Per-recipient link is a tracking wrapper over public content, not an access gate** | Forwarding to a decision-making room must work for strangers with no account (D-03)"; :51 (Edge Cases) — "the per-recipient link is a *tracking wrapper over public content*, not an access gate, so **a forward opens fine for a stranger with no account**". VERSUS :52 (Edge Cases) — "Link is shared publicly | An EPK **may contain rates and contact routes not meant for the world** | Needs expiry/revocation. See Q-02"; and Role Lens :17 — "Producer | Full | Generates a client-facing kit: discography, room, **rates**, turnaround, testimonials." Behavior :25 also assembles "for live pitches — tech requirements from domain 18". Note also that :52's cross-reference is mis-pointed: Q-02 is the PDF-export question; expiry/revocation is Q-03.
findings.forcedInvention: Whether EPK content is public (indexable, freely forwardable, no expiry needed) or confidential-but-unauthenticated (unguessable link, expiry, revocation). D-06 asserts the first as a ratified decision; the edge case asserts the second as a requirement. The choice determines whether a Producer's rate card is world-readable.
findings.downgradeRationale: Warning rather than blocking: 'public content' can be read as 'not access-gated' rather than 'already published', under which an unguessable expiring unauthenticated link satisfies both statements — a reading most implementers would reach. Q-03 tracks expiry/revocation, though not the public-vs-confidential status D-06 asserts as settled.
